You’ve got a problem? Excellent! Their revolutionary new system sends you to a nurse or physio who, with all due ceremony, refers you for a routine ultrasound… on bone. Because nothing screams medical excellence like ordering a scan that doesn’t actually work for the thing it’s meant to look at. Radiologist breaks the news that, surprise surprise, soundwaves bounce off bone. But that’s fine, because your details vanish into the void and follow-ups are as mythical as unicorns.

It seems the new system has been carefully modelled on a fairground queue: long, winding, and completely pointless—expertly designed to keep you shuffling along in false hope, believing you’re next in line. In reality, appointment times have tripled under Lie-bour while the illusion of efficiency is carefully maintained with buzzwords and laminated flowcharts.

And don’t even think about bringing up more than one problem at an appointment—how dare you try to be efficient or provide a full picture of your health. It’s strictly one problem per visit, thank you very much. Any attempt to link that backache with, say, the numbness you had six months ago? Forget it. They won’t check your history, because apparently Sherlock Holmes doesn’t work here. Continuity of care? Never heard of it.

Forget asking for a stronger dose or getting a repeat prescription set up—despite the hospital sending clear, typed-in-actual-English letters stating exactly that. But sure, let’s loudly discuss your bowel issues in front of a packed waiting room. GDPR? Never heard of her. In their world, privacy is just a quaint little myth, like professionalism or functioning healthcare.

And let’s not forget the two-and-a-half-year detour I took just to get referred for something because last time, an inconclusive ultrasound was apparently good enough to close the case. When I chased it up, I was told it had been too long, so guess what? Back to square one. That meant another round of pointless assessments and another three-month wait just to even get on the specialist’s radar.
